title: Lab 1 — Quiz 2
subtitle: Microbial Ubiquity — scientific method, safety, microbial groups

questions.prompt: Based on the Lab 1 safety rules, what should this student do before working with cultures?

options.text: Wear a lab coat over the shirt

questions.explanation: Safe hair: restrain hair to avoid contaminating your hair and your work.

why.B: Gloves are worn when instructed or when skin is broken; the issue shown is hair.
why.C: The rule shown is about hair; clothing must cover neck to knees.
why.D: Hair must be restrained, not disinfected.

questions.prompt: Which clothing rule is part of the micro lab safety policy?

options.text: Cover your skin from your neck to your knees
Wear shorts so lab coats fit better
Loose sleeves are fine if they are rolled up
Scarves and jewelry may be worn if tucked in

questions.explanation: Safe clothes: cover neck to knees; no dangling scarves, neckties or jewelry; avoid loose sleeves.

why.B: Skin must be covered from neck to knees.
why.D: No dangling scarves, neckties or jewelry.

questions.prompt: When must gloves be worn in micro lab?

options.text: When instructed, or anytime your skin is broken
Only during the Glo Germ activity

questions.explanation: Gloves: wear when instructed or anytime skin is broken; remove safely, discard properly, then wash hands immediately.

why.A: Glove use depends on instructions or broken skin, not equipment.
why.C: Gloves are required when instructed or when skin is broken.
why.D: Gloves are worn whenever instructed or when skin is broken.

questions.prompt: In the Microbial Ubiquity experiment, how is the plate inoculated?

options.text: Open the lid fully and press the swab into the agar
Leave the plate open on the surface you chose for 10 minutes
With the plate inverted, lift the agar half and wipe the swab across it in three directions
Drop the swab into the plate and close the lid

questions.explanation: With the plate inverted, lift the agar part, wipe the swab back and forth in three directions across the entire surface without gouging, then discard the swab in biohazard.

why.A: Don't gouge the swab into the agar; keep the plate inverted and lift only the agar half.
why.B: The protocol swabs a surface, then wipes the swab on the agar.
why.D: The swab is wiped on the agar and then discarded into the biohazard bag.

questions.prompt: Where on the plate are labels written?

options.text: On the outside of the bottom (agar half) of the plate
Inside the lid with a sterile marker

questions.explanation: Write your initials, lab day and time, and sampling location on the outside of the bottom of the plate.

why.B: Labels go on the outside of the bottom of the plate.
why.C: Labels go on the outside so nothing touches the medium.
why.D: Each plate is labeled with initials, lab day/time and sampling location.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a hypothesis is correct?

options.text: A hypothesis is the final conclusion of an experiment
A hypothesis must always be proven correct
A hypothesis cannot be formulated without first making observations
A hypothesis is a list of quantitative data

questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a proposed explanation for observations; it cannot be made without observations first, and it leads to testable predictions.

why.A: A hypothesis is a proposed explanation, tested by experiments.
why.B: Hypotheses lead to testable predictions and can be rejected (like the elephant in the box).
why.D: Data are collected; a hypothesis is a proposed explanation for observations.

questions.prompt: In the controlled experiment slide, sterile medium inoculated with known Streptococcus is the:
questions.explanation: Positive control: known organism, expected growth. Negative control: no organisms added, expected no growth.

why.B: The negative control has no organisms added and should show no growth.
why.C: The test culture is the patient's sputum specimen.
why.D: It's a control with a known expected result (growth).

questions.prompt: In the controlled experiment, what is the expected result for the negative control?

options.text: The same result as the sputum specimen

questions.explanation: The negative control (sterile medium, no organisms added) should show no growth — it confirms the medium wasn't contaminated.

why.B: Growth is expected in the positive control.
why.C: No organisms are added, so nothing should grow.
why.D: The test culture's result is unknown; the negative control should show no growth.

questions.prompt: What does 'ubiquitous' mean, as applied to microbes in the Microbial Ubiquity experiment?
questions.explanation: Ubiquitous = present everywhere. The experiment asks: where are microbes located?

why.A: Most microbes are benign or even beneficial.
why.C: Microbes are microscopic; colonies are what become visible.
why.D: Ubiquitous refers to location, not survival.

questions.prompt: Which group of organisms below is unicellular, prokaryotic, often extremophilic, and not known to cause disease in humans?
questions.explanation: Archaea: unicellular prokaryotes, pseudo-peptidoglycan walls if any, often extremophiles, archaella for motility, not known to cause human disease.

why.A: Many bacteria cause disease, and most have peptidoglycan walls.
why.D: Protozoa are eukaryotes and some are parasitic.

questions.prompt: This organism is a mold (a fungus). Most fungal cell walls are composed of:
questions.explanation: Fungi: yeasts or molds; most have chitin cell walls; absorb organic molecules; mostly nonmotile.

why.A: Peptidoglycan is the bacterial cell wall.
why.C: Cellulose is the cell wall of most algae.
why.D: Pseudo-peptidoglycan is found in some archaea.

questions.prompt: This organism is Spirogyra. Which group is it in?
questions.explanation: Algae: unicellular or multicellular, mostly cellulose walls, photosynthetic, not known to cause human disease (though some make toxins that concentrate in shellfish).

why.A: Protozoa lack cell walls; Spirogyra is a photosynthetic alga.
why.D: Helminths are multicellular worms in Kingdom Animalia.

questions.prompt: Which protozoan from the slides is able to photosynthesize?
questions.explanation: Protozoa absorb or ingest organic molecules; some, like Euglena, can photosynthesize.

why.A: Giardia is a parasitic protozoan, not photosynthetic.
why.C: Plasmodium is an obligate intracellular parasite.

questions.prompt: Protozoa, like the one shown, differ from algae and fungi because protozoa:
questions.explanation: Protozoa: unicellular eukaryotes, lack cell walls, move by flagella, cilia or pseudopods; free-living or parasitic.

why.A: Chitin walls are found in fungi.
why.C: Cellulose walls are found in most algae.

questions.prompt: Which statement about bacteria is FALSE?

options.text: They reproduce asexually by binary fission
Most have a cell wall made of peptidoglycan
Flagella and axial filaments are used for motility

questions.explanation: Bacteria are well known for causing disease, but most are benign or even beneficial.

why.A: True — bacteria divide by binary fission.
why.C: True — peptidoglycan is the typical bacterial wall.
why.D: True — these are bacterial motility appendages.
why.E: True — some derive energy from photosynthesis.
